And this is something that I would like to present to you for your consideration. Thank you. Page 3, first paragraph, third sentence, in English, it says, [In English] "Before the conflict was 93 percentage of Kosovo Albanians and 7 percentage non-minority communities including some 3.000 Kosovo Serbs who mostly lived in main town." [Interpretation] Mr. Haxhibeqiri, this is a publication called Municipal Profile of Djakovica dating from 2003. It was published by the OSCE mission in Kosovo. Is there any particular reason why you do not accept the percentage -- the number of 7 per cent as the non-Albanian population in the municipality of Gjakova?

utterances.speaker: Fuat Haxhibeqiri [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you I have never seen these statistics written anywhere. What sources do you refer to? You said the UNMIK or I believe they are approximate figures. There is no way how UNMIK can know accurately without a census being taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Very well. And how did you then come to this figure of 2 per cent of the Serbian population, if -- or the non-Albanian population, if the census had not -- was not carried out? How did you get to that figure of 2 per cent of the non-Albanian population?

utterances.speaker: Fuat Haxhibeqiri [Resumed]
utterances.text: I always refer to official figures. I have constantly seen such figures published.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Can you give me any publication where these figures were cited?

utterances.speaker: Fuat Haxhibeqiri [Resumed]
utterances.text: In all bulletins all the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis? Are you on your feet?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I am, Your Honour. I'm not sure how to go about this. I would just indicate within the document itself, although I agree with what Mr. Visnjic read about the 7 per cent, I see the chart below lists a percentage figure for January 1999, which is different than what it says in the text.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I don't know if it is different because I think that is -- well ...

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The percentage of Albanian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah. But the -- I don't think it is different because the 2 per cent does make sense as the Kosovo Serb population. Is that the figure you're pointing to, the 2 per cent?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: 3.000 is roughly 2 per cent. I don't think there is any argument about that. The question so far has been about the overall non-Albanian population which is being put at a higher figure.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, and the Albanian is listed at 98 per cent. Plus 2 is a hundred.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Indeed. Mr. Visnjic?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, that leads me to the conclusion, and I will ask the witness the following.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Other than Serbs in the municipality of Djakovica, were there any other inhabitants who were not Albanian?

utterances.speaker: Fuat Haxhibeqiri [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Montenegrins, Romas, and Bosnians.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Is there an ethnic community by the name of Ashkali?

utterances.speaker: Fuat Haxhibeqiri [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We call them Albanian Egyptians, but in the Kosovo plateau they are called Ashkali plateau.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Dukagjini plateau, correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: And you count them in the category of others, not as Albanians? Could you please reply? I'm now going to go step by step. Do you agree with me that there were about 3.000 Serbs in the municipality of Djakovica in January 1998?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters don't hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Could you repetition that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't work in the statistics section.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Haxhibeqiri, can you tell me how many Serbs are living now in the Djakovica municipality?

utterances.speaker: Fuat Haxhibeqiri [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Haxhibeqiri, can you tell me how many other ethnic groups, other than the Albanians, are living in the municipality of Djakovica now? Approximately, you don't have to give me the exact figures.

utterances.speaker: Fuat Haxhibeqiri [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Haxhibeqiri, I would like to ask page 7 to be shown, this same document, page 7. Before I put my question, I'm going to say to you that in this document, there is a list of NGOs active in the Djakovica municipality. On page 7, line 4, there is a reference to your organisation, the Council for the Defence of Human Rights and Freedoms, and the objectives of your organisation are referred to. Since you were president of that organisation I assume that it will not be difficult for you to recall the following. The objectives of your organisation are the collection of human rights violations data and report publication, training, seminars, promotion of independent media, election monitoring. I assume it's electronic media that's referred to. I'm sorry, election monitoring. And last but not least, minority rights protection. My question, Mr. Haxhibeqiri, is the following: Does your organisation deal with minority rights at all, or is this inaccurate, this objective of your organisation mentioned here?

utterances.speaker: Fuat Haxhibeqiri [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. Your question is irrelevant. I repeated it several times that we didn't have access to Serbian events, documents, and Montenegrin, but as far as the others are concerned, we tried to maintain an equitable stand towards all of them, as far as we could under the circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Does this pertain to the period after 1999 as well? I mean up to 2002 while you were president of the organisation. I'm referring to the period starting after June 1999 and up to 2002.

utterances.speaker: Fuat Haxhibeqiri [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you please repeat the question? What do you want me to answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Well, my question: Did your organisation deal with the protection of the human rights of minorities after June 1999, up to 2002?

utterances.speaker: Fuat Haxhibeqiri [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, exactly as it is said there.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Can you describe to me at least some of the activities that your organisation had in terms of minority protection in Djakovica?

utterances.speaker: Fuat Haxhibeqiri [Resumed]
utterances.text: We have organised seminars, we have held a catchup school with Albanian Egyptian community, accelerated schools, they are called. Whoever has come to our office to ask for assistance, we have provided that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Did you offer any help? Did you offer any help to the Serb community or the Montenegrin community?

utterances.speaker: Fuat Haxhibeqiri [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Free of charge, juridical assistance, legal assistance, we have provided to all of them who have come to our office and asked for it. After the war, no Serbs or Montenegrins have come to our offices for assistance. All the rest, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you, Mr. Haxhibeqiri. We will get to that again later. Let me ask you something else now. My next group of questions has to do with your work with the International Crisis Group. You described in detail how you worked with these forms and I wanted to ask you the following. Can you tell me how you conducted interviews? How many people were present? Let's start with that. Who would bring in a witness? Your organisation, your people, did they bring witnesses to the representatives of the ICG for them to be interviewed?

utterances.speaker: Fuat Haxhibeqiri [Resumed]
utterances.text: We addressed them. We went to villages by car, five of us, and the ICG representative who was present during the interviews. He was English usually. Can't remember the name. There were others too.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Yes. All right. What was it that you said, how many representatives of the ICG would usually be there? One?

utterances.speaker: Fuat Haxhibeqiri [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were two or three sometimes but usually there was one. As we divided ourselves in two groups, there was one in each group.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: So when there were several representatives of the International Crisis Group there, they would usually be subdivided into groups, if there were several interviewees at a given time? Did I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: Fuat Haxhibeqiri [Resumed]
utterances.text: They came time after time to monitor the activity.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: All right. When you came to villages, I'm talking about the post-war period, where did you usually conduct interviews? Was it in houses, at a particular place like a local commune centre in a village?

utterances.speaker: Fuat Haxhibeqiri [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was in private houses, in the courtyards, in their rooms, if the weather was not good.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Yes. I assume that you always tried to have decent working conditions to have a table and electricity for a computer?

utterances.speaker: Fuat Haxhibeqiri [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time there were no computers in villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Let's leave computers aside. You wanted to have the right conditions for working?

utterances.speaker: Fuat Haxhibeqiri [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, accommodation was not important at the time.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Says the witness in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When the house was not burned, we would get into the premises of the house, to conduct the interview inside if it was raining, but most of the interviews was conducted in the courtyard of the houses we went to. There were no computers at the time. There was no electricity. The houses were burned massively.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Very well. You said that you cannot remember the name of any International Crisis Group representative; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Fuat Haxhibeqiri [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have their names recorded but it's seven years now so I've forgotten them. I can't remember them off the top of my head, but I can fax them to you if you want them. I can send them to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Haxhibeqiri, could you please tell me whether you interviewed a person by the name of Bajram Bucaliu?

utterances.speaker: Fuat Haxhibeqiri [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I can't remember. Maybe he's in my file but I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Do you recall interviewing a person by the name of Muharem Dashi?

utterances.speaker: Fuat Haxhibeqiri [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Do you recall interviewing a person by the name of Merita Deda?

utterances.speaker: Fuat Haxhibeqiri [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Do you recall interviewing a person by the name of Shukri Gjegjaliu?

utterances.speaker: Fuat Haxhibeqiri [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Do you remember interviewing a person by the name of Behar Haxhiavdija?

utterances.speaker: Fuat Haxhibeqiri [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't interviewed Behar.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Did you speak with Hani Hoxha?

utterances.speaker: Fuat Haxhibeqiri [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: And did you interview him for the International Crisis Group?

utterances.speaker: Fuat Haxhibeqiri [Resumed]
utterances.text: Others, but not Hani.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Very well. And did you speak with a person by the name of Bedri Hiseni?

utterances.speaker: Fuat Haxhibeqiri [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Kuci or Kuqi?

utterances.speaker: Fuat Haxhibeqiri [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can talk about one or two because I have interviewed hundreds but I cannot remember all their names.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: I'm not trying to get you to recall all but at least to remember one person that you interviewed, Osman Kuci or Kuqi. We don't have an answer here. I don't have the answer in the transcript. This is why I'm asking you again.

utterances.speaker: Fuat Haxhibeqiri [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Dout Imeraj?

utterances.speaker: Fuat Haxhibeqiri [Resumed]
utterances.text: No,

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: And Mehmet Avdili?

utterances.speaker: Fuat Haxhibeqiri [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Do you recall -- oh, there is no reply. Can you please repeat your answer for Mehmet Avdili? It's not in the transcript. This is why I'm asking you.

utterances.speaker: Fuat Haxhibeqiri [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Do you recall where you talked with Merita Deda? Was that in her village or was that in Djakovica? I know a lot of time has passed since then but --

utterances.speaker: Fuat Haxhibeqiri [Resumed]
utterances.text: In her home or in the courtyard, if she is from Guske or Korenica. It seems to me it's from Guske.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: During that conversation, there was a representative of the International Crisis Group present. One of them or more of them?

utterances.speaker: Fuat Haxhibeqiri [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Fuat Haxhibeqiri [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember. I met Merita at the hotel because I had forgotten who she was, and I don't think I have interviewed Merita.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Did you speak with her or not? Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: Fuat Haxhibeqiri [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to see who filled in her form. That's how I would know if I spoke with her or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Very well. But when you were filling in the questionnaires and the section of the form where it says the person who filled in the form, did you put in your name there or somebody else's name? When you filled in the questionnaire, there is a section there where -- let me just put the question to you. There is a section on the form of the person that is conducting the interview, am I right? When you read your interview form, that was one of the sections?

utterances.speaker: Fuat Haxhibeqiri [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The name of the interviewer, the name and the surname of the interviewer is there.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: So that's why I'm waiting.

utterances.speaker: Fuat Haxhibeqiri [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm also waiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Did you write your own name in that part of the form? You conducted the interview. Did you put one name in that part or several names?

utterances.speaker: Fuat Haxhibeqiri [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said earlier I'm not sure whether -- whether it was me who conducted the interview or whether I've completed the name. What are you trying to say is that what are you asking me to do?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: I'm not interested in Merita Deda?

utterances.speaker: Fuat Haxhibeqiri [Resumed]
utterances.text: Merita is here. Ask her.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Says the witness in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: I'm going to ask her but I'm just asking you did you interview any of the other 100 people there, when you did whose name would you enter in that particular place where it says person who inter -- conducted the interview?

utterances.speaker: Fuat Haxhibeqiri [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're not clear in what you're asking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you if you are the interviewer, if you are conducting the interview, please read out in that form of yours who was the interviewer, what does it say there under "interviewer," the person who conducted the interview? That will do.

utterances.speaker: Fuat Haxhibeqiri [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whom? I said it will be one of our team. You may ask Merita who was she interviewed by. Why are you insisting on this with me?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: I'm not asking about Merita any longer.

utterances.speaker: Fuat Haxhibeqiri [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have the file of Merita here with me. If I had the file with me, I would have shown you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Haxhibeqiri, you're not being asked about her at the moment. You're being asked in general, and the general question is being asked by reference to the document you brought with you. Now, if you look at the document which you showed us earlier, in the place where the note should be made of the name of the person conducting the interview, in that particular form, what name has been noted?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is what I'm looking for here. If he knows, let him tell me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, no. You're being asked to tell us what name has been recorded as the name of the person who conducted the interview. Now, look at the form and tell us the answer to that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Are you -- if you're asking about this interview, this is not Merita's file. This is the file of somebody else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We know that. You're not being asked about Merita Deda. You're being asked in general about the conduct of these interviews. Do you understand that? And you're being asked about how they were conducted in general but by reference to the document which you brought to court. Now, look, please, at that document and tell us whose name has been inserted at the place where you put the name of the person conducting the interview.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The name of the interviewer there is Besa Morina. It's member of the council for the defence of human rights and freedoms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Haxhibeqiri, there it was a bit of a misunderstanding but we have resolved that and I think you've just answered my question right now. So let me add on to this: You did not enter the name of the representative of the ICG, who was with you at that time or near you at the time when the interview was conducted, right? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Fuat Haxhibeqiri [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've got all their names. I may send them to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Haxhibeqiri --

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I hear that again there is something missing from the transcript. Mr. Haxhibeqiri said "me," [phoen] no. That is to say that they did not enter the names of the representatives of the International Crisis Group who were with them at the time and who were near them at the time. I would like this to be clear in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note that many times there are several speakers speaking at the same time and all the booths cannot hear them.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Should I put the question again?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We note that that was the answer. Carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Haxhibeqiri, did you ever work for the OSCE, you or your organisation? Did you ever work for the Organization for European Security and Cooperation?

utterances.speaker: Fuat Haxhibeqiri [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Again, the answer was not recorded. Ah, now it is. Thank you. I'll go back to the form. I hope it's not too much trouble for you to look at the form that you showed the Judges a few moments ago, and at the same time I would like to ask to show on the monitor 3D02. That's an exhibit from earlier on that was admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm not going to ask the witness about the document that's on your monitors right now but I did ask for it to be shown because of something that I would like to compare. I'm going to ask him about what is written in his form.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: So in your form, as you explained --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speaker please speak into the microphone?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, today, on pages 22 and 23, the witness read the form that is before you now. And there is a rubric here stating describe the perpetrators of the crime and then it said the army of Yugoslavia, the police, paramilitaries, and civilians. Or civilians.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The form we have on the screen is from Merita Deda?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right, Your Honour, because that form says something different. I'm telling you now what the witness said that his form said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Indeed, but this is not one of the forms of his organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, please. Your Honour, it is a form of his organisation that was disclosed to us as a form and as an electronic form of the International Crisis Group.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, we had --

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I beg your pardon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We had this problem before with the source of this but this as I understand it was disclosed in the context of the evidence of either Mitchell - it was probably Mitchell - and wasn't said, I think, at that stage to have come from the CDHRF that we are hearing about from this witness. It was material which had been gathered by the OSCE and then -- and the explanation sort of hung in the air, had become incorporated into other material on the ICG database or alternatively I think they had been given some job of managing the data. Now, it doesn't follow immediately, does it, that this is as compiled by Mr. Haxhibeqiri's organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [In English] May I explain?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Haxhibeqiri, first of all, what I'm discussing now with the judges has nothing to do with the question that I'm going to put to you so please rest assured that it has nothing to do with what I'm going to be asking you. I'm going to talk to the judges about a completely different matter now.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] According to Rule 66(A)(ii), the OTP disclosed to us a total of nine statements that were provided to us as material from the International Crisis Group.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In that material, that we received these nine statements, one of the statements is this one, the one that you see before you right now, and that is Merita Deda's statement which was disclosed to us as material from the ICG. I'm not claiming that that it's material from the ICG. That is from the Prosecution asserts. That is why I put this document before this witness now. There is yet another document that was disclosed to us as an OSCE document. It was disclosed to us later, and it so happened that it contains the same text. But I'm not going back to that form now. I am now talking about the form of the International Crisis Group that was disclosed to us as such. If the Prosecutor tells us now that this is not material of the ICG, then I can withdraw my question. But for the time being, this is what we got from them, only a definition stating that this is material of the International Crisis Group and that it falls under Rule 66(A)(ii). And by the way, today we filed a motion regarding that particular question and I'm sure that we will discuss it later on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Hannis, do you accept that this was disclosed on the basis that it was from the International Crisis Group.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would premise my remarks with indicating that Mr. Stamp is more familiar with this particular issue because of dealing with Ms. Mitchell he will but I'm looking at the form that's on the screen right now, which is K 0213894, and the top line says, "ICG database incidents." There is another document that Mr. Visnjic made a reference to with which is K 0529762, which is referred to as the OSCE materials. It's my understanding that we received materials from both of those agencies to manage that data. What I understand is internally we created a data base and put that information in. Not in the raw form in which it was received but into a database that we created and transported the raw data. But with regard to the witness's form, my understanding is the forms that he used with the Council for the Defence of Human Rights and Freedoms was in Albanian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Set that aside for the moment. It's the provenance of this that matters. And the point Mr. Visnjic is making is that this has been handed to him as a document, which was an ICG document. Now, do you dispute that?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm note sure if it was as ICG document or information that came from ICG documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Well, it's not clear as far as the Prosecution are concerned. Therefore you can proceed, Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: With respect, we were told that ICG was protected under Rule 70 before the break and now it's disclosed to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm going to come back to you later. Let's just get the questions finished first of all. Yes Mr. Visnjic, carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: So I'm going back to page 22 and 23. Mr. Haxhibeqiri, we are coming back to the questions for you now. In your own form, you described as the possible options for a witness's answer that crimes were committed either by the army or the police or paramilitaries or civilians; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Fuat Haxhibeqiri [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Is there any other option, any other possibility in your form? Again, I don't have an answer. I'm going to ask you again.

utterances.speaker: Fuat Haxhibeqiri [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know but if you know anything let me know. For the moment, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. I have to ask you yet again because your answer has not been recorded. So is it correct that in your form there are only the following options for perpetrators of crimes, the army, the police, paramilitaries, and civilians?

utterances.speaker: Fuat Haxhibeqiri [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What was your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Hold on. What was your answer to that question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was asked to read the text? And whether I -- whether I agree with the drafting of that text, of the ICG, and I said yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No. The question is whether in your form, that's the form your organisation was using, there are only the following options for perpetrators of crimes: The army, the police, paramilitaries and civilians. Now, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Visnjic?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Haxhibeqiri, these options were offered as options in the case of all crimes, murder, kidnapping, and relocation or rather forcible deportation.

utterances.speaker: Fuat Haxhibeqiri [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Haxhibeqiri, I'm going to ask you, as an experienced investigator because you conducted so many interviews, had this research of yours been carried out, say, in the Roma community and if they were given this kind of form, had they been given this kind of form, and had the Roma moved out because their homes were bombed by NATO, do you see any possibility, any option that they could actually fill out in this form of yours?

utterances.speaker: Fuat Haxhibeqiri [Resumed]
utterances.text: In some instances, yes. They came to the office, to the ICG and reported their cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Are you telling me that there are forms where NATO bombing was put in as a reason for relocation or deportation or people moving out?

utterances.speaker: Fuat Haxhibeqiri [Resumed]
utterances.text: Deportation was a forceful one and not because of fear of NATO bombing. Albanians did not flee the country out of fear. Can you please let me finish?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Could you answer the question, please?

utterances.speaker: Fuat Haxhibeqiri [Resumed]
utterances.text: NATO did not instill any fear among the Albanians, as you are trying to present it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Haxhibeqiri, please listen to what you're being asked. It's not for to you choose to -- what you want to tell us. Your obligation here, I'm afraid, whether you like it or not, is to answer the questions that are being put to you. Now, you've been here for the best part of three days, more than two days certainly, and you must understand by now what is the procedure. You're an intelligent person. And I'm not going to be deflected from trying to get to the truth of these matters because you choose to answer different questions from the ones that are being asked. This series of questions is about the form that's being used. And the point is being asked of you, where is the option in your form, for anyone who comes to the office, whether they be a Roma, an Albanian, or anyone else, to say, "I left my home because of fear of NATO bombing"? Now, can you answer that, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. None of them did that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's not the question. You're answering a different question. The question is, was there a place in your form in which you would -- you would --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Realtime transcript read in error "werpgs"] No. In the form there was no place. I think I explained that because I was several times -- you have the form here, you can see it. You can look it for yourselves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You see, Mr. Visnjic, there is equally a point to be made here that many of these questions are simply asking for answers that are already obvious and they are all matters for argument later. And because the question -- the answer to the question is obvious, the witness probably thinks, What on earth is he asking this for? It must be something more subtle that is behind these questions? Let's get on with the job. So I think you're both here to some extent at fault in the way in which this is being presented. You only need to look at the form to know that there is no point in it that says, Were you driven out by fear of NATO bombing.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Your Honour, I don't have his form so I am restricted to that degree. Another thing I'd like to say, if you look at his form -- may I please continue or rather finish? If you look at his form and if you look at the form that is in front of you and if it is correct that that's two forms come from the same organisation, then it is obvious that somebody either translated differently the form that is in front of us now in electronic form or in his form there is absolutely no possibility for a different answer. That is what I'm putting to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, well, it's all far too complicated for this witness to deal with. It's not even clear who conducted the interview that the Deda form relates to. It's a typewritten version that looks like it's been compiled at a later date from other material that was handwritten. So I don't know where we are going on this. I think we are going around in circles, frankly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Might I state for the purposes of the record here that at page 54, line 16, part of the witness's answer has been ascribed to Judge Bonomy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, that's certainly noted. But please carry on now, Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Haxhibeqiri, you said to us that in some cases, if I understood your answer correctly, the Roma did come to your office, or to see the ICG, and they reported cases of their leaving their homes because of NATO bombing. So that is correct, right?

utterances.speaker: Fuat Haxhibeqiri [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't know of any statements to that effect, to prove that they left because of NATO bombing. I don't know of any such cases. There may have been some sporadic cases of people declaring that they have left because of fear of bombs.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Did you note down such cases anywhere?

utterances.speaker: Fuat Haxhibeqiri [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which cases do you mean? Can you be more explicit, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: I'm referring to your statement that there may have been some sporadic cases of people declaring that they had left because of fear of bombs. My question is, did you record such cases?

utterances.speaker: Fuat Haxhibeqiri [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In cases of children who were under great pressure and suffered traumas. They couldn't bear with the bombing in the Ivica Brod [phoen] village where the military base was situated.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Did you submit this information in any form to the International Crisis Group or the office of the OTP?

utterances.speaker: Fuat Haxhibeqiri [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which information?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Information that [In English] "Children under great pressure and suffered traumas, they couldn't bear with the bombing in the village where the military base was situated." [No interpretation] --

utterances.speaker: Fuat Haxhibeqiri [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm answering you. You asked me whether there were people who were afraid of NATO bombs and I said yes. I don't know of any written records. I'm just saying that children were afraid of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: But you just told --

utterances.speaker: Fuat Haxhibeqiri [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I can tell you that no one was afraid of NATO.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: But in answer to my question, as to whether you recorded any such cases, your answer was: Yes, in cases of children who were under great pressure and so on and so forth. So you recorded those cases somewhere. That was my question. Your answer was affirmative. Now I'm asking you the following. Let me complete my question. Did you inform the crisis group of this in any way or the OTP of this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: Fuat Haxhibeqiri [Resumed]
utterances.text: They have their own representatives there, the International Crisis Group has prepared a report. I don't know if you have read that report. They have often drawn conclusions about that situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Haxhibeqiri. Thank you. We'll move on. Very briefly, please take your statement, on page 4, paragraph 2 of the B/C/S version, paragraph 1 of the English version, and paragraph 1 of the Albanian version. Mr. Haxhibeqiri, before we move on to this, another question about the ICG. Did you receive any kind of training before you started working for the ICG? I mean training in interviewing witnesses.

utterances.speaker: Fuat Haxhibeqiri [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Who trained you?

utterances.speaker: Fuat Haxhibeqiri [Resumed]
utterances.text: The ICG staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Fuat Haxhibeqiri [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Now we are coming to paragraph 1 in the Albanian version of your statement. In the second part of that paragraph you mention a person by the name of Dragutin Prentic and in your statement you say the following --

utterances.speaker: Fuat Haxhibeqiri [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not in the first paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's the first paragraph on page 4.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, I found it. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: You refer to an incident in which he wrote an article?

utterances.speaker: Fuat Haxhibeqiri [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not me. It was the witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: After the publication of this article, employees of the post office were sacked. My question is, in what year was that article published and to what period does this statement refer?

utterances.speaker: Fuat Haxhibeqiri [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Haxhibeqiri, you're telling me that Dragutin Prentic published an article in 1999 and that after the publication of that article, all the Albanians who were employees of the post office were sacked? Did I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: Fuat Haxhibeqiri [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The year is not marked at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: No. I'm asking you in what year that article was published.

utterances.speaker: Fuat Haxhibeqiri [Resumed]
utterances.text: This article was published on the day one day before the violent repressive measures were introduced in the post office of the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: What year was that?

utterances.speaker: Fuat Haxhibeqiri [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I can't give you the exact time but I mentioned the period from 1990 to 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Haxhibeqiri.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, does that -- is that an accurate record of the answer? You initially said this was 1999. When is it you say it occurred?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. I said from the 1990s to 1999. That was the period when the roles changed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But you're being asked about a particular article written by Dragutin Prentic, which you say was the day before, the day before Albanian employees of the post office were sacked. Now, when was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said approximately between 1990 until 1993. That was a period when this happened, I believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Haxhibeqiri --

utterances.speaker: Fuat Haxhibeqiri [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: You conclude that this man had a large political influence based on a newspaper article published in 1993. Do I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: Fuat Haxhibeqiri [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not only on one article, but he wrote several articles, well in advance of the closing down of an organisation or -- well, in advance before repressive measures were introduced there, he published those articles in Jedinstvo newspaper, a Serbian newspaper.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Well, let me ask you the following, then: Did that man have any political influence in 1999?

utterances.speaker: Fuat Haxhibeqiri [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: And you base your claim on these newspaper articles published between 1990 and 1993?

utterances.speaker: Fuat Haxhibeqiri [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He was appointed as director of Djakovica Radio at that time. When he was appointed director, that was called Djakovica Radio at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: When is it -- hold on. When do you say he was appointed director of Djakovica Radio?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 1990.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And did he still hold that position in 1999?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, all the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Serbs had that position. There were no Albanians there. And this is one of the repressive bodies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Haxhibeqiri. You go on to say in that same paragraph that witnesses saw that in Meja on the 27th of April he was recording the entire scene with a camera. Will you tell me who was it who saw him in Meja with his camera?

utterances.speaker: Fuat Haxhibeqiri [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I have to go through my files to give you the names of the persons who saw him doing that and who knew him personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Very well. I hope we will be able to clarify this in the course of the trial. Now, please answer the following question. You say in the morning he wore a mask and in the afternoon he didn't. Could you clarify this?

utterances.speaker: Fuat Haxhibeqiri [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is always according to the witnesses who saw him wearing a mask, a black mask, in the morning, with slits for the eyes to record the event, but in the afternoon he didn't wear the mask. Yes. This is how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this may be a convenient time for a break. I will have five minutes at the most for this witness after the break, depending on his answers, but not more than five minutes, I anticipate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think you should carry on and let's try to finish your cross-examination before lunchtime.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Haxhibeqiri, tell me the following: If I put the following to you, that your organisation is accusing almost all the Serbs in Djakovica of having committed war crimes in order to prevent and limit their return, would I be right in saying this?

utterances.speaker: Fuat Haxhibeqiri [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you repeat the question, please? I'm not clear about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Haxhibeqiri, would I be correct in asserting that your organisation is accusing almost all the Serbs in Djakovica of having committed war crimes in order to prevent and limit their return to Djakovica?

utterances.speaker: Fuat Haxhibeqiri [Resumed]
utterances.text: The return to Gjakova is restricted by the number, large number, of victims, 1254 victims. Their return is not possible because of the unburied 280 corpses that are found in Serbia. Or somewhere else, you may know better. This is why they cannot return to Serbia. The crimes they have committed. They don't have a clean conscience.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Haxhibeqiri, this refers to all the Serbs? Am I correct? In Djakovica municipality.

utterances.speaker: Fuat Haxhibeqiri [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean all those who have committed crimes, both Serbs and Montenegrins.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It says, they are not able to return to Serbia. Could we have that clarified at line 21, line 21, page 61, line 21. "This is why they cannot return to Serbia."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Haxhibeqiri, you explained that it was because of the number of victims, corpses found in Serbia, they don't have a clean conscience. That is why they cannot return to -- and where were you referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because of the large number of victims, 1254.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Where is it you say they cannot return to for that reason? It's been recorded that you said they cannot return to Serbia for that reason. Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I was asked why they cannot return to Gjakova and I showed why they cannot return to Gjakova because of the crimes they have committed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. That clarifies the position. Now, when we return after lunchtime, I will give you, Mr. O'Sullivan, the opportunity, if you wish, to ask questions about the whereabouts or existence of these documents, if there is to be any discussion about it, that's a separate platter but if you feel that there is a need to explore in evidence the location or identity of documents, then you can do that. Then the Bench will have a number of questions for the witness depending on certain clarification I may seek, first of all, from Mr. Hannis, and we will take matters from there. So we will -- I'm sorry, Mr. Hannis?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have I think two questions on redirect, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Indeed, indeed. But if we start asking questions, then that may give rise to further cross-examination before you even get to that stage, I'm afraid. It just depends on the extent to which it's appropriate for us to do so. Just one matter before we adjourn, Mr. Haxhibeqiri, there are certain documents you've referred to in your evidence which could be made available. One of them was a document you referred to as having in the hotel which was details of the powers of the Crisis Staff. Do you now have that document with you? We will deal with it this afternoon. As long as you've got it there, we'll deal with it this afternoon. So we will resume at ten minutes past 2.00. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.39 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. O'Sullivan?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, we don't wish to pursue the matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Haxhibeqiri, the document you showed us just before lunchtime, could we now have that document, please? Now, the document has been handed over is a document which is dated the 31st of March 1999. Is this set out in the Serbian language or the Albanian language?

utterances.speaker: Fuat Haxhibeqiri [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Serbian language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: At first glance, it does -- at first sight, even to me, it does appear to me to be along the lines suggested but obviously it would have to be translated. So what we will do with this document is mark it for identification as a court exhibit and that will be marked for identification subject to translation and any comments that parties wish to make after it's translated. Now, does anyone have any objection to take to that course of action?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: None from me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. The next matter, Mr. Haxhibeqiri, is the list you mentioned today of a number of people -- I hope I'm not misrepresenting the figure, I think it was 37, was it, who were killed at Jablanica, which you were asked about in a different context. Was it 37 people you said had been killed there?

utterances.speaker: Fuat Haxhibeqiri [Resumed]
utterances.text: 27 but -- 27 but not in Jablanica but in the Asim Vokshi street, Asim Vokshi street in the city of Gjakova.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, sorry, I've given you the wrong figure and that's probably what's misleading. When Mr. Cepic started his cross-examination this morning, he was asking you about events in Jablanica and he was talking about the deaths of 16 civilians. And one answer you gave was that you had a list of 40 Albanians killed in that village, I think 40 Albanians killed in that village.

utterances.speaker: Fuat Haxhibeqiri [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's the list of all those who were killed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, can I see that document?

utterances.speaker: Fuat Haxhibeqiri [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, this is a much longer document than one containing the names of 40 victims. This has a total of 586. So what is this document?

utterances.speaker: Fuat Haxhibeqiri [Resumed]
utterances.text: In both lists you will find the names of about 40 from -- 40 people from Jablanica who were killed there, and you -- it's alphabetically ordered and where it starts with J you will find the names of the people who were killed at Jablanica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, it's alphabetical -- both lists are alphabetical according to the name of the person, the victim, not according to the place.

utterances.speaker: Fuat Haxhibeqiri [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not according to the place, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And I don't see that -- I don't see the name Jablanica on the one I'm looking through at the moment. So what -- just give me a second.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It may be under the Albanian name of Shqiponja, which was the name given to Jablanica after the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I see that in fact one of the documents has reference to persons from Jablanica. However, the matter is obviously much more complicated than the simple question of a list with 40 names of victims from Jablanica, so what the Trial Chamber will do is return these two documents to the witness. It may be that the Prosecution will see some advantage in investigating this further and if there was something that could be of assistance in the interests of justice presenting that to the Trial Chamber but we do not intend to pursue this particular issue further at this stage. Does anyone have any objection to that course of action? Thank you. So that means there is one document to be given a court exhibit number which presumably will be number 1. Never mind the 00s. It will be IC1. In fact do we need the I? Is it just C1?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [In English] Excuse me, Your Honour. [Interpretation] In connection with this document, which Your Honour just referred to, number 1, C1, may we obtain copies?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. The copies will be distributed immediately they can be made.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, I think that leaves just the one matter but just how complex that will be has yet to be determined. Mr. Hannis, it was plain in the witness's evidence-in-chief that he felt he had much more personal knowledge of events or at least knowledge that got close to personal experience of killings in particular, that he had not had an adequate opportunity to recount because of the way in which the statement had been taken. In the full knowledge of that state of affairs, you decided not to explore the matter further. And there may be a number of reasons for that. I fully appreciate it. The Chamber, though, is concerned that if he does have personal knowledge of matters which are relevant to the indictment, that he ought to be given an opportunity to explain what that is. But there is no point in us entering into that area with him if in fact his personal knowledge relates to matters which are not relevant to the charges here. Now, was it for that reason that you did not pursue the matter?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, with regard to killings, I had understood from questions that had been asked and answers given, that while he may have gone out and seen dead bodies at scenes of killings, perhaps within hours of the killings actually having occurred, he had not personally witnessed the actual killing itself and so that's why I didn't explore it any further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Now, Mr. Haxhibeqiri, you've heard my discussion with Mr. Hannis. We are anxious that you should have an opportunity to relate to the Trial Chamber anything of which you have personal knowledge, that's direct experience, that you think would assist us as long as it is relevant to events between the 20 -- well, I think in broader terms probably relevant to events in 1998 and up until June 1999. But in particular, personal knowledge of the killing of anyone that you consider to be a criminal act. Now, I don't want to hear from you very general statements about your knowledge. I want to know if there are particular events that are not referred to in your statement which you have direct personal knowledge of, and can now tell us of. And in the course of your evidence you mentioned the killing of four people, which was not referred to in any detail in your statement. You also said that that was not the whole extent of your knowledge. Now, can you explain to me -- Mr. Sepenuk, unless there's a -- something important, I wonder if --

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Your Honour, very respectfully, I think there is. Just a minute or so, this gentleman was called at as a Rule 92 bis witness and our expectation was, under Rule 92 bis, that the testimony would be confined to the statement and we think 92 bis on its face only provides for evidence that is within the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, we've already discussed this and I can't see for the life of me how you make that interpretation of Rule 92 bis where it says clearly, "the Chamber may admit in whole or in part the evidence of a witness in the form of a written statement."

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: The reason I say that, Your Honour, is 92 bis A, where it says "a Trial Chamber may admit in whole or in part," as Your Honour says, "the evidence of a witness in the form of written statement in lieu of oral testimony." In lieu of oral testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: So our understanding is, Your Honour, that the statement -- that it's confined to the statement and any testimony over and above that is not permitted within the terms of 92 bis. And my only other comment Your Honour is that, with all respect to Your Honour's need to get the facts of this case, asking this witness, and I say most respectfully to this witness who has given very discursive, generalised, almost advocacy kinds of statements, to expect that he's going to confine himself pinpointedly and clearly and succinctly to a particular area I think might be too much to expect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, what that amounts to is a challenge to the ability of this Trial Chamber to control the evidence it seeks from a witness, and your concern about that is quite unfounded, and therefore, I reject that suggestion. The first point you make is one that I really don't understand. The rule says the Trial Chamber may admit in whole or in part the evidence of a witness in the form of a written statement in lieu of oral testimony. The bit that's in writing has got to be in lieu of oral testimony. That doesn't mean to say in lieu of everything oral. Doesn't mean that. And in any event, the Trial Chamber has a specific right and I'm looking for the rule to ask any question it wishes. If you look at Rule 85,(B), "It shall be for the party calling a witness to examine such witness in chief but a judge may at any stage put any question to the witness."

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: I grant that's the general rule, Your Honour, but where Rule 92 bis specifies we think the particular governs over the general. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I reject your interpretation of -- of -- as do my colleagues, of your interpretation of Rule 92 bis.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, may I just touch upon one aspect which seems to be very important to me? It has to do with something Your Honour mentioned briefly yesterday. We have a situation here where the witness was not properly prepared. The previous Prosecution team preparing this witness obviously did not do a good job and now we have a situation where this witness is presenting facts to Your Honours which, in the seven years at least that the Prosecution investigation into these events has been ongoing, should have been investigated. They were not investigated, however, and we now have a situation where the witness is presenting some very serious facts referring to murders and so on, and we may even get facts from him referring to the acts and conduct of the accused. We now have completely new facts which the Defence is hearing for the first time, after the beginning of the witness's testimony. And there is no way that the Defence can test the credibility of everything that these witnesses are putting forward. There is a whole series of rules referring to disclosure, the main point of which is to enable the Defence to properly deal with all the evidence. We may hear something today or tomorrow from this or another witness and the Defence will not be in a position to challenge this properly because it will not have the proper tools and materials at its disposal. So the right of the accused to fair and just proceedings should not be brought into question. Of course, this falls within the discretionary powers of Your Honours, but we may be now coming close to a line where the right to a fair trial might be compromised. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, without expressing any further view on the quality of preparation of this witness, it seems to the Trial Chamber that even if, indeed particularly if, there was a failure to obtain from a witness important, relevant evidence in the pre-trial or prior to the pre-trial stage of the case, that this Trial Chamber would be failing in its duty to the interests of justice if it were not to explore what it is that the witness might be able to say. There are many mechanisms available to the Trial Chamber to ensure that the interests of the accused are protected in the light of what develops, particularly in a case that's likely to last for a couple of years, and there is plenty of time to resolve any difficulty that may arise. Whether a trial is fair or not is to be determined at the end of the trial, unless there is some glaring breach that could never be rectified at any later stage. So I hear what's said. My colleagues hear what's said. We reject the suggestion that it's inappropriate for the Trial Chamber to explore this matter any further and we will respect the interests of the accused and the interests of justice whenever we intervene to ask questions in the course of this trial. Now, Mr. Haxhibeqiri --

utterances.speaker: Fuat Haxhibeqiri [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I want to be clear first of all about this. At any stage in 1998 or 1999, did you personally see any person being killed as the result of an act of violence?

utterances.speaker: Fuat Haxhibeqiri [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have seen killed people but not people being killed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What is the earliest time, as far as you could judge, after any person had been killed, that you saw the body?

utterances.speaker: Fuat Haxhibeqiri [Resumed]
utterances.text: Within 12 hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Was that by chance or because you had been contacted in some way to notify you of the death?

utterances.speaker: Fuat Haxhibeqiri [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were in the streets, some 50 metres away from my home. As I was passing by I saw them there. Seven corpses I've seen. I knew three of them but the other four, no. Later on, I also learned their names.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are these seven corpses you saw on the one occasion or are we talking about more than one incident?

utterances.speaker: Fuat Haxhibeqiri [Resumed]
utterances.text: Within the same day, and they were -- one of the corpses stayed there for four days. The others were removed within the same day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And are these matters not referred to at all in your statement?

utterances.speaker: Fuat Haxhibeqiri [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, you made an assertion at one stage that your statement of matters of which you have personal knowledge could fill a hundred pages and you may even at one stage have said more than that. Bearing in mind it's your personal experience that we are interested in, are there any other events that you feel you ought to tell us of that are of a similar, as to which your knowledge is similar to the knowledge you have of the one you've just mentioned?

utterances.speaker: Fuat Haxhibeqiri [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just hold on. I'm getting no interpretation.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Sorry. "I have seen with my own eyes a convoy on the morning of the 24th of March, in the 27th of March, when these forces came to the Blloku i Ri neighbourhood, when -- and they set the neighbourhood alight. They burned more than 10 houses. They killed eight persons or seven to be more accurate, rather, seven, and they arrested 11 other people."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That is referred to in your statement. That matter we do not need to explore any further. So let's lay that one aside. Now, is there any other event?

utterances.speaker: Fuat Haxhibeqiri [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The case of Cabrat. I've seen fighting take place from the roof of my house, from a distance of 300 metres.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What is the date of that event?

utterances.speaker: Fuat Haxhibeqiri [Resumed]
utterances.text: 7th of May. Until the 11th of May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, again, that is an area that's already been explored in evidence and you have been -- had an opportunity to expand upon that already. Is there any other event?

utterances.speaker: Fuat Haxhibeqiri [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're talking about things which I have personally experienced?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Fuat Haxhibeqiri [Resumed]
utterances.text: During my work at the Human Rights Council, there were cases coming to my office, especially the beginning of 1998 up until one day before the bombing started, we've had cases --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Again, I think that's a matter that has been adequately explored. The Prosecution have chosen how to present that -- their evidence on that subject and therefore, I don't think we need to go into that one any further. That's been a decision made by the Prosecutor. Okay. So leaves the one thing, the one event that requires, I think, further exploration, where you say that you saw, I think it -- was it eight people you said? Yes, when you saw the corpses on the one day. Now, could you tell us more about how you came upon these corpses and what you know about the event that led to their being killed or dead?

utterances.speaker: Fuat Haxhibeqiri [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were civilians. They were taken in the street while fighting was going on in the Cabrati hill between the KLA and the Serb/Montenegrin forces. They entered the houses, and whoever they found there they tortured or killed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, how do you know that? How have you learned of that?

utterances.speaker: Fuat Haxhibeqiri [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw that with my own eyes. I saw them setting fire to houses, during the day and at night, all the time. And on the next day I heard of the victims or maybe one day after. So as time went by I learned the number of the dead people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And what was that number?

utterances.speaker: Fuat Haxhibeqiri [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean the overall number? 100 -- roughly 106.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: For the avoidance of doubt, give us again the date of that event or these events.

utterances.speaker: Fuat Haxhibeqiri [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the 7th to the 11th of May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And now confine your subsequent answers to the seven corpses. Tell us how you saw these, where you saw them, and what you know of how the seven corpses came to be corpses.

utterances.speaker: Fuat Haxhibeqiri [Resumed]
utterances.text: One of them is called Ali Beqe Rama. I saw his body 50 metres away from my house. It was lying in the middle of the street. Two brothers, Humaj, they were called, I saw them in a store which is about 50 metres away from my home. They had put the bodies inside the store. They were full of blood. I could hardly recognise them. One of them had the identity paper on him and it was through that that I identified him. When I left the store they told me that the two brothers were killed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Who do you mean "they" told you that the two brothers were killed?

utterances.speaker: Fuat Haxhibeqiri [Resumed]
utterances.text: People who were there, people from that neighbourhood. They had learned of that killing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. And the others? You said there were four others.

utterances.speaker: Fuat Haxhibeqiri [Resumed]
utterances.text: In another lane close by to my aunt's house, when I was going to visit my aunt, I saw the bodies in the street. My aunt has -- had emptied the house and I saw the bodies from a distance of about 30 metres. And later, I found out about their names.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And how many bodies are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: Fuat Haxhibeqiri [Resumed]
utterances.text: Seven.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, in the lane close to your aunt's house how many bodies?

utterances.speaker: Fuat Haxhibeqiri [Resumed]
utterances.text: Four.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Fuat Haxhibeqiri [Resumed]
utterances.text: Four.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And what were the names?

utterances.speaker: Fuat Haxhibeqiri [Resumed]
utterances.text: One is called Florenc Sulejmani. The others I don't know but I have records of them as victims, killed on that date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And do you know anything of how any of these four were killed?

utterances.speaker: Fuat Haxhibeqiri [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were killed -- they were shot dead.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And I should have asked you that in relation to the two brothers and to Ali Beqe Rama. How were they killed?

utterances.speaker: Fuat Haxhibeqiri [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the same way, with bullets. I saw both the brothers, I could identify both of them myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Excuse me if I asked you a little personal question. The question is: Is this your name or -- you add Haxhi to it which means having performed a pilgrimage? Have you been -- have you been for hajj? That's what I was thinking. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Fuat Haxhibeqiri [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, if Defence counsel wish to discuss their position, we are happy to adjourn for that purpose. If you consider it appropriate to cross-examine the witness on any matter raised in this, then you should do so, and then -- Mr. O'Sullivan?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Perhaps a ten-minute adjournment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. We'll adjourn and we'll resume at five past 3.00. --- Break taken at 2.53 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. O'Sullivan, can you indicate the position or is someone else going to do it? Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, usually I'm not in charge of administrative mat ores but since I was cross-examining Mr. Haxhibeqiri first my colleagues empowered me to speak in the name of everybody. And as I understood my colleagues, our position is that we would like to reserve our right to call this witness again if -- because we have to conduct the investigation on these matters. And if we find something that is different than this witness is claiming in this additional questioning or part of his statement, we would kindly ask this Chamber to allow us to call this witness again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think it would be entirely appropriate for you to make an application in suitable circumstances, so I acknowledge that that -- this may be one. But it depends obviously on what develops between now and then. For the moment you're content to leave the matter as it is?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Hannis, to re-examine?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I just had one topic I wanted to touch on and perhaps to reduce the possibility of the witness having to come back.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: It pertains to the Crisis Staff document, Mr. Haxhibeqiri, that you brought in and gave to the Judges this afternoon. Can you tell us how you came to be in possession of that document? When did you get it, who did you get it from?

utterances.speaker: Fuat Haxhibeqiri [Resumed]
utterances.text: I found this document in the offices of a communal assembly. The people who entered the offices after the war collected them and brought this document to my office for me to have it in my archives.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: When did that happen?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you know when in 2000?

utterances.speaker: Fuat Haxhibeqiri [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: Fuat Haxhibeqiri [Resumed]
utterances.text: Don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I'm a little unclear. Was it you personally who found that document at the communal assembly or someone else?

utterances.speaker: Fuat Haxhibeqiri [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not I personally who found it but others brought it to me, the staff of the commune assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you recall anybody by name from that group who brought it to you?

utterances.speaker: Fuat Haxhibeqiri [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Kosovo protection corps, who at that time were called KLA, they have this document as well --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: Fuat Haxhibeqiri [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- because they were the ones who had access to documents both in the MUP and in other places after the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And that copy that you brought to court, had you kept that in your offices from the time you received it in 2000 until you brought it here this week?

utterances.speaker: Fuat Haxhibeqiri [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I don't have any other question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hannis. Any other questions? Well, Mr. Haxhibeqiri, that completes your evidence. Thank you for coming to the Tribunal to give it. You're now free to leave.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Hannis, who is to be next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's Lizane M-a-l-a-y -- M-a-l-a-j. I believe -- she's outside, I hope.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: In fact, perhaps she should just be kept for a moment. There is an issue over the admissibility of the statement of the last witness which I ought not to be overlooked at this stage. Now, remind me, who was it who initially took exception? Mr. Ivetic, was it you?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. O'Sullivan, I believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It was Mr. O'Sullivan. I take it you maintain the position, do you?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Yes, we do, Your Honour. We object to the admission of certain portions of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Pages 6 to 9?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That will be dealt with along with the other outstanding decisions and hopefully in the course of next week.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: The only additional thing I would wish to draw your attention to is 92 bis(A)(ii)(b) which we say applies to the -- our standing objection to this and other similar statements and notably the Abrahams 92 bis statement. We say that the circumstances surrounding the statement make it unreliable and unsafe for admission and that the prejudicial value of it outweighs any probative value it may have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's have the witness now, Mr. Hannis. Mr. Sepenuk?

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, we join in the motion made by Mr. O'Sullivan. And just to make it clear, the latter part of the statement referring to the thousand interviews and the interviews resulting from that we claim that the law is -- is similar. We invoke the law respecting as seen, as told and under orders to preclude the admission of that part of the statement, and we also again, Your Honour, claim, and I know Your Honour has rejected that, but that any oral evidence over and above what was in the statement, we claim, should not be considered by the Trial Chamber. One final thing, Your Honour, and that concerns one of the exhibits. It's a booklet called Serb genocide upon Albanian culture at Gjakova. Your Honours will recall those are the pictures of certain mosque and other monuments, since there was some personal knowledge of those pictures we don't have any objections to that. We would ask you though to ignore -- to delete the booklet term Serb genocide. This is not a genocide case. Nobody in this case has been charged with genocide. Genocide has a specific meaning, as Your Honours well know, usually killings with intent to destroy in whole or in part a national ethnic, racial or religious group. We don't have that in this case. It's not charged and I think it's inappropriate to have that in the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We'll --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If I may, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a question, please, I'm so sorry, Mr. Hannis, I'm sorry.
